100%;\"\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\n\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eRL training and agent evals whose environments are \u003cstrong\u003eKubernetes\u003c/strong\u003e -\nclusters, charts, in-cluster workloads - need thousands of isolated,\nresettable worlds. Not one sandbox, and not a cold \u003ccode\u003ekind\u003c/code\u003e cluster per\ntrial. Booting a fresh Kubernetes cluster takes ~30 s and full RAM\nper copy. k7d boots it \u003cstrong\u003eonce\u003c/strong\u003e, then forks the live cluster in\n~100 ms; forks share memory until they diverge, so 50 copies cost\ndirty pages, not 50 × full guest RAM.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe same engine is also a great \u003cstrong\u003efork-first VMM\u003c/strong\u003e when your unit is a\nsingle VM sandbox (including docker-in-VM): blazing-fast warm forks with\nfaithful snapshotting of memory, disk, processes, and networking. For\nrunning that at scale - Kubernetes orchestrating your sandboxes, plus a\nCLI / API / Python SDK for agents - see the sibling project\n\u003cstrong\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://github.com/Katakate/k7\"\u003eKatakate k7\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e100% open‑source\u003c/b\u003e (Apache‑2.0). Cold-booting a fresh cluster\ntakes ~30 s and a full RAM bill per copy; k7d boots once, then\ncopies share memory until they diverge.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e🔁 \u003cstrong\u003eThe cluster keeps running after the fork\u003c/strong\u003e - no agent restarts,\nno broken TLS, no \"please wait while Kubernetes comes back.\" Each\ncopy looks identical to the original from the inside.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e🌲 \u003cstrong\u003eBuilt for AI agents that explore many worlds\u003c/strong\u003e - fork a branch,\ntry something, keep the winners, throw away the losers. The agent\ndecides what to keep; k7d enforces RAM and disk budgets so the tree\ndoesn't eat the machine.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e🧊 \u003cstrong\u003eAlso a blazing-fast VM-sandbox VMM\u003c/strong\u003e - warm-fork a single guest\nin ~5 ms with faithful memory / disk / process / network state.\nIdeal for docker-in-VM and any workload that needs resettable\nisolated machines, not only whole k8s clusters. Pair with\n\u003ca href=\"https://github.com/Katakate/k7\"\u003eKatakate/k7\u003c/a\u003e when you want k8s\norchestration + Python SDKs on top.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e🔬 \u003cstrong\u003eWe use formal methods where they pay off\u003c/strong\u003e - \u003ca href=\"https://model-checking.github.io/kani/\" rel=\"nofollow\"\u003eKani\u003c/a\u003e\non selected \u003ccode\u003eunsafe\u003c/code\u003e / arithmetic paths, and\n\u003ca href=\"https://aeneasverif.github.io/\" rel=\"nofollow\"\u003eAeneas\u003c/a\u003e→Lean on the tree\nbudget/eviction model. Not a claim that everything is proven -\ndetails \u003ca href=\"#formal-verification\"\u003ebelow\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e🪶 \u003cstrong\u003e≤30k lines of Rust for the VMM + shim\u003c/strong\u003e - small enough to read\nand audit. Deliberately not a kitchen-sink VMM.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e✅ \u003cstrong\u003eEvery number here is a CI assertion\u003c/strong\u003e - not a one-off benchmark\npaste. If member A starts from a colder cache, a different etcd\nrevision, or a half-ready Deployment than member B, the reward gap is\nnoise, not signal. A k7d fork is a copy of the live machine - same\nmemory, same disk, same in-cluster TLS sessions, same kube-apiserver\nstate. Every member of the group begins from a \u003cstrong\u003ebyte-identical\u003c/strong\u003e\nworld, then diverges only because of what your policy did.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThat is the difference between \"we reset the env\" and \"we cloned the\nuniverse.\"\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eHow your agent talks to the tree\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-how-your-agent-talks-to-the-tree\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: How your agent talks to the tree\" href=\"#how-your-agent-talks-to-the-tree\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eYour training loop owns rewards and policy. k7d owns environments and\nbudgets. The agent talks JSON-lines over a Unix socket\n(\u003ccode\u003e/run/k7d/k7d.sock\u003c/code\u003e). The verbs you actually need:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cmarkdown-accessiblity-table\u003e\u003ctable\u003e\n\u003cthead\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eYou want to…\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eCall\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/thead\u003e\n\u003ctbody\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eStart from a warm VM or live cluster\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003etree_create\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003etree_create_cluster\u003c/code\u003e / \u003ccode\u003etree_adopt_cluster\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eOpen N parallel rollouts from one checkpoint\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003etree_fork_batch\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eTry again from an earlier node without destroying it\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003etree_rollback\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003ePin a winner so budget pressure can't kill it\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003etree_protect\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eDrop a losing subtree\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003etree_prune\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eEnforce RAM/disk caps now\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ccode\u003etree_auto_evict\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003c/markdown-accessiblity-table\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eA thin Python client that covers exactly this loop lives in\n\u003ca href=\"/Katakate/k7d/blob/main/examples/cluster-tree-search\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003eexamples/cluster-tree-search/\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/a\u003e. Treat\nit as the template for wiring your GRPO trainer - not as a finished\nSDK. You do need to know\n\u003cem\u003ewhy\u003c/em\u003e a 100 ms cluster fork is even possible, because that is the\nproduct.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eMemory is shared until someone writes.\u003c/strong\u003e Guest RAM lives in one file.\nA fork pauses the source for a moment, notes which pages changed since\nthe last checkpoint, maps the child's memory as a copy-on-write view of\nthe parent's, and copies only those dirty pages. Everything else is\nshared. That is why 50 forks of a cluster fit in 64 GB: you pay for\ndivergence, not for the base.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eThe cluster does not reboot because the network lies consistently.\u003c/strong\u003e\nEach cluster lives on its own private Linux bridge. A fork gets a\n\u003cem\u003enew\u003c/em\u003e bridge with the \u003cem\u003esame\u003c/em\u003e guest IPs and MAC addresses as the source.\nFrom inside the guest, nothing moved - same addresses, same ARP cache,\nsame TLS certs, same established TCP - so kubelet, the CNI, and the\ncontrol plane keep running. Separate bridges mean forks cannot see each\nother. Without this, every fork would force a kubelet restart and a\n~1-2 s agent restart per node, and the 100 ms claim would be\nimpossible.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eForks Live copy-on-write fork\nrequires parent and child memory to be mappings in the same process.\nGuest→host isolation is still KVM; isolation \u003cem\u003ebetween sibling forks\nof the same tenant\u003c/em\u003e is weaker than Firecracker's\none-jailed-process-per-VM. k7d is built for fleets of \u003cem\u003eyour own\u003c/em\u003e\nenvironments, not hostile multi-tenant isolation between forks.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat survives a fork:\u003c/strong\u003e everything inside the forked set -\nin-cluster TLS, established TCP between member VMs, disk state.\nGuest clocks are reset so time does not jump backwards.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat doesn't:\u003c/strong\u003e TCP to the outside world (the far end never\nforked). Forks keep their in-cluster addresses; only the\nhost-facing identity is new.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eSingle host, x86_64 Linux + KVM only.\u003c/strong\u003e Cross-node fork is on the\nroadmap. Does not build on macOS/Windows.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eYoung project.\u003c/strong\u003e ≤30k LOC for the VMM + shim, one primary test\nmachine, no security audit yet. <p dir="auto">RL training and agent evals whose environments are <strong>Kubernetes</strong> -
clusters, charts, in-cluster workloads - need thousands of isolated,
resettable worlds. Not one sandbox, and not a cold <code>kind</code> cluster per
trial. Booting a fresh Kubernetes cluster takes ~30 s and full RAM
per copy. k7d boots it <strong>once</strong>, then forks the live cluster in
~100 ms; forks share memory until they diverge, so 50 copies cost
dirty pages, not 50 × full guest RAM.</p>
<p dir="auto">The same engine is also a great <strong>fork-first VMM</strong> when your unit is a
single VM sandbox (including docker-in-VM): blazing-fast warm forks with
faithful snapshotting of memory, disk, processes, and networking. For
running that at scale - Kubernetes orchestrating your sandboxes, plus a
CLI / API / Python SDK for agents - see the sibling project
<strong><a href="https://github.com/Katakate/k7">Katakate k7</a></strong>.</p>

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Why k7d</h2><a id="user-content-why-k7d" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Why k7d" href="#why-k7d"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>⚡ <strong>Fork a running Kubernetes cluster in ~100 ms</strong> - and pack
<strong>50 copies on one 64 GB box</strong>. Cold-booting a fresh cluster
takes ~30 s and a full RAM bill per copy; k7d boots once, then
copies share memory until they diverge.</li>
<li>🔁 <strong>The cluster keeps running after the fork</strong> - no agent restarts,
no broken TLS, no "please wait while Kubernetes comes back." Each
copy looks identical to the original from the inside.</li>
<li>🌲 <strong>Built for AI agents that explore many worlds</strong> - fork a branch,
try something, keep the winners, throw away the losers. The agent
decides what to keep; k7d enforces RAM and disk budgets so the tree
doesn't eat the machine.</li>
<li>🧊 <strong>Also a blazing-fast VM-sandbox VMM</strong> - warm-fork a single guest
in ~5 ms with faithful memory / disk / process / network state.
Ideal for docker-in-VM and any workload that needs resettable
isolated machines, not only whole k8s clusters. Pair with
<a href="https://github.com/Katakate/k7">Katakate/k7</a> when you want k8s
orchestration + Python SDKs on top.</li>
<li>🔬 <strong>We use formal methods where they pay off</strong> - <a href="https://model-checking.github.io/kani/" rel="nofollow">Kani</a>
on selected <code>unsafe</code> / arithmetic paths, and
<a href="https://aeneasverif.github.io/" rel="nofollow">Aeneas</a>→Lean on the tree
budget/eviction model. Not a claim that everything is proven -
details <a href="#formal-verification">below</a>.</li>
<li>🪶 <strong>≤30k lines of Rust for the VMM + shim</strong> - small enough to read
and audit. Deliberately not a kitchen-sink VMM.</li>
<li>✅ <strong>Every number here is a CI assertion</strong> - not a one-off benchmark
paste. If a latency claim drifts, a test fails. Methodology:
<a href="/Katakate/k7d/blob/main/docs/blog/2026-08-07-k7d-cluster-fork-benchmark.md">the benchmark write-up</a>.</li>
</ul>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Quickstart</h2><a id="user-content-quickstart" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Quickstart" href="#quickstart"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">You need a Linux <strong>amd64 / x86_64</strong> host with KVM (<code>/dev/kvm</code> present) -
same ISA (<code>amd64</code> is the Debian name; tarballs use <code>x86_64</code>). No arm64
build yet. Rust and Docker are required to build from source. Prebuilt
release tarballs are produced by <code>make release</code>
(<code>k7d-v*-x86_64-linux.tar.gz</code> + <code>install.sh</code>).</p>

<p dir="auto">The demo forks a live 3-VM cluster, scores branches, keeps the winner,
prunes the losers, and prints the fork wall-clock. To put real
Kubernetes pods <em>inside</em> those VMs (<code>runtimeClassName: k7</code>), see
<a href="/Katakate/k7d/blob/main/HACKING.md"><code>HACKING.md</code></a>. Full docs (API reference, installers) will
ship separately - this README is the product pitch + getting started.</p>

<p align="center" dir="auto"><sub>The whole run, 7×. Delete fails. A lab is sacrificed. The door holds.</sub></p>
<p dir="auto">Someone planted a miner in a Deployment that looks like a helper.
The real app (<code>k7-victim</code>) is fine. Kimi K3 does not touch
production first - it clones the cluster three ways and tries delete,
scale-to-zero, and “just watch.” The miner comes back every time.
So it forks <em>again</em> from the copy that already knows delete is a lie.
One of those labs restarts k3s to catch the respawner and is left
broken on purpose. No rollback. Another hangs an admission lock on
the name <code>node-agent</code>; recreate comes back denied. Only that pair of
moves is replayed on the source. Soak: still gone. Victim 2/2.
Tetragon clean.

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Using k7d for GRPO / agent tree search</h2><a id="user-content-using-k7d-for-grpo--agent-tree-search" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Using k7d for GRPO / agent tree search" href="#using-k7d-for-grpo--agent-tree-search"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">If you already have Kubernetes tasks or scenarios (a Helm chart, a
set of YAML manifests, an eval harness that talks to a kube-apiserver),
the shape is:</p>
<ol dir="auto">
<li><strong>Boot the scenario once</strong> - bring up your cluster (or adopt a
running one that k7d already hosts) and wait until it is in the
state you want every rollout to start from.</li>
<li><strong>Root a tree at that checkpoint.</strong></li>
<li><strong>For each GRPO group (or tree-search step):</strong>
<code>fork_batch(N)</code> → run your N policies against the N copies → score
→ <code>protect</code> the winners, <code>prune</code> the losers → let the daemon
<code>auto_evict</code> under your RAM/disk budget.</li>
<li><strong>Roll forward</strong> from a protected winner when you want the next
generation to start from a better state, or <code>rollback</code> to an
earlier node when you don't.</li>
</ol>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Why byte-identical starts matter for GRPO</h3><a id="user-content-why-byte-identical-starts-matter-for-grpo" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Why byte-identical starts matter for GRPO" href="#why-byte-identical-starts-matter-for-grpo"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">GRPO (and most group-relative methods) compare rewards <em>within a
group</em>. If member A starts from a colder cache, a different etcd
revision, or a half-ready Deployment than member B, the reward gap is
noise, not signal. A k7d fork is a copy of the live machine - same
memory, same disk, same in-cluster TLS sessions, same kube-apiserver
state. Every member of the group begins from a <strong>byte-identical</strong>
world, then diverges only because of what your policy did.</p>
<p dir="auto">That is the difference between "we reset the env" and "we cloned the
universe."</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">How your agent talks to the tree</h3><a id="user-content-how-your-agent-talks-to-the-tree" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: How your agent talks to the tree" href="#how-your-agent-talks-to-the-tree"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">Your training loop owns rewards and policy. k7d owns environments and
budgets. The agent talks JSON-lines over a Unix socket
(<code>/run/k7d/k7d.sock</code>). The verbs you actually need:</p>
<markdown-accessiblity-table><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>You want to…</th>
<th>Call</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Start from a warm VM or live cluster</td>
<td><code>tree_create</code> / <code>tree_create_cluster</code> / <code>tree_adopt_cluster</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Open N parallel rollouts from one checkpoint</td>
<td><code>tree_fork_batch</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Try again from an earlier node without destroying it</td>
<td><code>tree_rollback</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Pin a winner so budget pressure can't kill it</td>
<td><code>tree_protect</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Drop a losing subtree</td>
<td><code>tree_prune</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Enforce RAM/disk caps now</td>
<td><code>tree_auto_evict</code></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></markdown-accessiblity-table>

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">How it works (the non-obvious bits)</h2><a id="user-content-how-it-works-the-non-obvious-bits" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: How it works (the non-obvious bits)" href="#how-it-works-the-non-obvious-bits"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">You do not need to be a VMM engineer to use k7d. You do need to know
<em>why</em> a 100 ms cluster fork is even possible, because that is the
product.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Memory is shared until someone writes.</strong> Guest RAM lives in one file.
A fork pauses the source for a moment, notes which pages changed since
the last checkpoint, maps the child's memory as a copy-on-write view of
the parent's, and copies only those dirty pages. Everything else is
shared. That is why 50 forks of a cluster fit in 64 GB: you pay for
divergence, not for the base.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>The cluster does not reboot because the network lies consistently.</strong>
Each cluster lives on its own private Linux bridge. A fork gets a
<em>new</em> bridge with the <em>same</em> guest IPs and MAC addresses as the source.
From inside the guest, nothing moved - same addresses, same ARP cache,
same TLS certs, same established TCP - so kubelet, the CNI, and the
control plane keep running. Separate bridges mean forks cannot see each
other. Without this, every fork would force a kubelet restart and a
~1-2 s agent restart per node, and the 100 ms claim would be
impossible.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Forks live in a tree the daemon manages under budget:</strong></p>
<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="base cluster ──► fork A ──► fork A1   (protected: winner)
             ├─► fork B                (pruned: low reward)
             └─► fork C ──► rollback ─► fork C'"><pre lang="text" class="notranslate"><code>base cluster ──► fork A ──► fork A1   (protected: winner)
             ├─► fork B                (pruned: low reward)
             └─► fork C ──► rollback ─► fork C'
</code></pre></div>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Three tricks that had to be right</h3><a id="user-content-three-tricks-that-had-to-be-right" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Three tricks that had to be right" href="#three-tricks-that-had-to-be-right"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">These are the kinds of bugs that silently break "byte-identical."
<a href="/Katakate/k7d/blob/main/CHALLENGES.md"><code>CHALLENGES.md</code></a> has all 56; these three are the
headline ones:</p>
<ol dir="auto">
<li><strong>Device writes are invisible to the hypervisor's dirty log.</strong>
Block devices in k7d write guest memory from userspace. The
hypervisor only sees CPU writes - so a fork taken after disk I/O
would resurrect <em>pre-I/O</em> bytes on those pages (silent corruption).
Fix: track device dirty pages ourselves and merge them into the
fork bitmap, and drain in-flight I/O before the bitmap is read.
(<a href="/Katakate/k7d/blob/main/CHALLENGES.md">CHALLENGES.md #43</a>)</li>
<li><strong>A restored guest with a blank timer chip freezes time.</strong> After
fork, the interval timer was left unprogrammed - no timer
interrupts, <code>CLOCK_REALTIME</code> stuck, and Kubernetes quietly parks.
Fix: re-arm the timer (and reset the paravirtual clock) on every
restore. (<a href="/Katakate/k7d/blob/main/CHALLENGES.md">CHALLENGES.md #40</a>)</li>
<li><strong>Identical IPs only work if the L2 domains are separate.</strong> Replay
the source's addresses onto a fresh bridge per fork. Same view
from inside; no conflicts across forks. That is the zero-restart
trick above.</li>
</ol>

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Kubernetes feature support</h2><a id="user-content-kubernetes-feature-support" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Kubernetes feature support" href="#kubernetes-feature-support"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Inside a forked cluster (your GRPO scenario)</h3><a id="user-content-inside-a-forked-cluster-your-grpo-scenario" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Inside a forked cluster (your GRPO scenario)" href="#inside-a-forked-cluster-your-grpo-scenario"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">This is the k3s that lives <em>inside</em> the VMs you fork. The fork engine
is <strong>N-node</strong> (<code>tree_create_cluster(vm_count)</code> / adopt any live set) -
there is no hard-coded 3. The CI fixture that proves the headline
numbers is a 3-node control plane with flannel + kube-proxy and a real
in-cluster Deployment. That <strong>default profile</strong> keeps stock k3s add-ons

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Security model & limitations</h2><a id="user-content-security-model--limitations" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Security model & limitations" href="#security-model--limitations"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<ul dir="auto">
<li><strong>One daemon, many VMs, one address space.</strong> Live copy-on-write fork
requires parent and child memory to be mappings in the same process.
Guest→host isolation is still KVM; isolation <em>between sibling forks
of the same tenant</em> is weaker than Firecracker's
one-jailed-process-per-VM. k7d is built for fleets of <em>your own</em>
environments, not hostile multi-tenant isolation between forks.</li>
<li><strong>What survives a fork:</strong> everything inside the forked set -
in-cluster TLS, established TCP between member VMs, disk state.
Guest clocks are reset so time does not jump backwards.</li>
<li><strong>What doesn't:</strong> TCP to the outside world (the far end never
forked). Forks keep their in-cluster addresses; only the
host-facing identity is new.</li>
<li><strong>Single host, x86_64 Linux + KVM only.</strong> Cross-node fork is on the
roadmap. Does not build on macOS/Windows.</li>
<li><strong>Young project.</strong> ≤30k LOC for the VMM + shim, one primary test
machine, no security audit yet. Small surface by design.</li>
</ul>
